en: Homage to Śiva and to Śakti, to the Bindu and to the Eternal One,
to the Guru, to Gaṇeśa, and to the wise Kārttikeya.
Having extracted from the ocean of the Siddhānta these three—known as Bindu, Śakti, and Śiva—in order for the virtuous to always bear them in their hearts, throats, and ears; SRtp_2 //
Therefore, I bind these jewels together with threads of words;
for that reason, the virtuous should forgive me, as there is no malice toward a servant.
Because it colors all principles (tattvas) through passion and the like,
and because it is to be sustained by the intellect of the lords (īśvara) and the Śivas within their respective domains.
And for men, through the mass of unimpeded and noble rays,
as well as by the provision of desired jewels, the [states of] *bindu* and so forth are established in the teaching of Śiva.
The collection of reality proceeds by relying upon the Three Jewels;
this path is attained and is described in six ways by the Supreme Lord.
This very doctrine is the seed for the three [stages] of initiation, consecration,
and the various yogas, as well as for the obligatory and occasional rites.
Through the awakening to that [Ātman], there arise gnoses, supernatural powers, and even liberation;
this very state is the supreme pinnacle known as liberation, resulting from the investigation of the individual self (aṇu).
This should be heard through the words of the authoritative teacher, reflected upon through logical reasonings,
and meditated upon by those whose souls have been awakened by the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*) via the path of yoga.
In this context, the established tenet is the word of a reliable authority (āptokti), because Śiva alone is the possessor of such authority;
for there is no one equal to him in bestowing the attainment of the highest good.
The final conclusion alone is the true conclusion; everything beyond that consists of prima facie arguments.
Śiva alone is the authoritative one; all others besides Śiva are considered inauspicious.
The established doctrine is followed by the virtuous who have been purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta);
by others, however, it is reviled out of their own arbitrary will, as if it were a scripture for bound souls (paśu).
For the fragrance of musk is not obstructed by men;
rather, it is established by its causes and is always inhaled by the fortunate.
And by the Vedantas, the Kula traditions, and others as well,
it is taught that for those deluded by [the notion of] bliss, consciousness is endowed with bliss.
The profundity of the great ocean of consciousness can be discerned by the wise only if,
upon plunging into it, one does not emerge from the waves of supreme bliss.
Therefore, O Lord, all this has been declared here in the most excellent of all streams;
one should then comprehend it with eyes turned upward and face directed upwards.
One should also examine its causes according to the treatises;
for in this matter, even a vast and sharp intellect does not prevail without purity.
Who knows by themselves, without the Siddhānta, these three jewels that are supramundane, subtle, and hidden by Śiva? (SRtp 18)

Who, by means of their wisdom, knows those causes that are enemies shrouded in the blinding darkness of fallacious reasoning, as well as yoga— characterized as both "with seed" and "seedless"— in that same way?
The established doctrine, when practiced by the virtuous, bestows all desires situated within the mind of the practitioner, just like a trusted wish-fulfilling gem.
Having cultivated that [tradition], I too shall conduct an investigation here concerning this power of the *bindu* which has Śiva as its locus; therein, the *bindu* is first described.
That which is the pure path from which it is born, wherein it abides, and wherein it dissolves—
that is the Bindu called Paranāda, the cause of Nāda, Bindu, and the phonemes.
Having crossed the ocean of māyā and shattered the great bolt of karma,
those who have not yet reached the abode of Śiva are the *vijñānakevalas* of three kinds.
The lords of knowledge and ignorance, preceded by Paśu, are the Sadāśivas;
therein, the eastern ones are the arms of Knowledge, consisting of Mantras and Vidyās according to their names.
These Vidyeśvaras, who are to be commanded, number seven crores;
their cities, Vāma and the others, are situated in the ether one after another.
Those who have newly arisen are flourishing with subtle bodies, enjoyments, sense organs, and so forth;
the intermediate ones, whose impurities are stilled, are the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) possessing the splendor of Śiva.
Free from the impurities that obstruct their authority, they have taken refuge in the reality of the Lord;
their own powers blossom through contact with the rays of the sun of Śiva.
Those eight [worlds] preceded by Ananta are superior in qualities in successive order; likewise, there are cities for them there, and Ananta is their supreme lord.
In those cities, there were the *aṇavas* (individual souls), nor others who were their manifestations;
there were also others equal to Sadāśiva, authorized for the duties of the Lord (*pati*).
Having reached the summit of the path once the Supreme Lord has become gracious,
their reality, O dear one, is born, adorned with the cities, enjoyments, and so forth.
Those [deities] who preside over Sadāśiva are also called Sadāśivas;
this path, together with the worlds and the enjoyers, consists of eighteen [levels].
And it is taught that the multitude of principles beginning with Sadāśiva is pure,
produced by Śiva, and has the eternal material cause as its source.
Because it is subject to transformation, just as a jar is;
and since this [body] is likewise so, even though it is made of earth, it would be a jar whose material cause is illusion.
Because they possess both destruction and origination, and likewise because they are subject to transformation,
whatever entity arises is illusory, just like a magical trick.
Maheśvara declares that arising and destruction are illusory properties;
for the transformation of things occurs through the relinquishing of their prior state.
The attainment of another state is like milk becoming curd, and curd becoming whey; in that process, the state of whey is thus defined.
For neither curd nor milk is [perceived] in their prior state;
indeed, a single entity exists in its state of being, first as milk and then as curd.
Subsequently, just like curd, illusion (māyā) is the imperishable material cause of both real and unreal entities, due to its manifold transformations.
Therefore, a valid illustration is well-established with the specified qualifications:
neither illusion, nor God, nor an atom, nor power belongs to the Pure Path.
Therefore, the *bindu* is obtained as the remainder;
for such is the illusion (*māyā*) of those [beings] when agitated by Anantatejas.
She gave birth to the entire collection of principles, beginning with water and ending with earth,
by virtue of her impure insentience and her nature as the path of *māyā*.
Because it is accompanied by suffering through the succession of the impurities of *māyīya* and *kārmāṇava*,
and because it is the object of enjoyment for all individual souls (*aṇu*) through the arising of transformations (*pariṇāma*).
Since Māyā is pervasive within the insentient, subject to transformation, and provides the body and other attributes for the production of the *kalās* and so forth; SRtp_43 //
One who is dependent on another will surely be led by that other, just as gold is led by a smith in the work of producing a crown. (SRtp 44)
This very [consciousness], being the domain of conceptual cognition,
is agitated by the Lord of the Infinite, just as clay is by a potter.
Conceptual cognition belongs to consciousness because it is permeated by sound;
that sound, moreover, is fourfold due to the distinctions of *vāk*, *vaikharī*, and so forth.
The Blessed One Ananta, whose body is Vidyā, is considered the agitator for the sake of perceiving the meaning of the Infinite, arising from the agitation of the *bindu*. (SRtp 47)
And that [state] of Māyā is called the principle of Bindu by the learned;
therefore, Maheśvara is likewise not derived from Māyā as its material cause.

Because of consciousness, because of non-activity, and because of transformation—for these reasons, the self (ātman) and its power (śakti) are to be known as such; the detailed exposition of this will be stated right here.
From this as well, a drop [of the soul] is inferred from the observation of inequality;
for some individuals are seen to be endowed with little knowledge and action.
But others, superior to them, are omniscient and powerful;
they consider the *pudgala* to be conscious, eternal, and devoid of transformation.
If there were modification, there would be the state of being insentient and impermanent, like a jar or a wall;
and likewise, consciousness is the power belonging to those two which are themselves unchanging.

That which exists in many ways arises through the power of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), by which consciousness, though atomic, perceives objects such as māyā and the rest when they are conjoined with it.
And that *bindu*, which possesses manifold functions, is variegated due to its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
the diversity of the atom does not arise independently of karma.
Even the variety of experience occurs through that [consciousness] which is dependent on [the body],
since it is by means of this that one undergoes the diverse enjoyment of karma, such as sandalwood and other things.
If that very [nature] were to perform that [action], what would be the use of those [causes]? Let them be discarded;
for the activity of all beings has as its cause the taking up and the abandoning [of objects].
They say that the imperishable sky is something superior even to the enjoyment and authority of those who possess the peerless sovereignty of the Śivas.
Just as space is the cause of the elements and so forth for the hosts of luminaries,
so indeed is the *bindu* the cause of what is called conceptualization within the various states of conceptual cognition.
By delineating its own various modifications through their mutual interpenetration, it attains consciousness;
yet this is not a mental impression (saṃskāra) termed "cultivation" (bhāvanā), because it exists as direct perception (adhyakṣa).
For the formative forces (saṃskāras) are indeed characterized by memory and do not fall within the scope of our direct perception;
nor is there a transformation of consciousness, because [consciousness] can exist even beyond illusion.
Likewise, the Lord of Knowledge, Ananta, having overcome Māyā by means of his splendor,
then brings forth creation, possessing a conceptualizing consciousness.
"Because it possesses agency while being atomic, it is like a person who is our servant.
Others, however, are experts in the doctrine of the transformation of the modes of activity (*vṛtti*). (SRtp 62)
The teachers explain this [self] with different qualifications:
"This one is the agent of transformation (pariṇāma), but not of activity (vṛtti); therefore, it is so. (SRtp 63)
"He who knows, 'This very thing, when agitated by me in such a way, will certainly accomplish the desired end'— he is the capable agent of transformations."
This dharma occurs in things that undergo transformation and possess functional activity;
for in this way, everyone perceives [reality] when all conceptual constructions have been shaken off.
The world perceives an object through conceptualization;
otherwise, even after an infinite [time], it would be preceded by a cognition permeated by words.

And if it were held that everything here is cognized, and this [consciousness] performs [the cognition], then one would think "I cognize with conceptualization" due to the conceit of awareness. (SRtp 67)
The abode of the *bindu* is considered to be like a hut for a cloth;
therefore, even within non-conceptual awareness, the Lord presides over the *bindu*.
The Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara) does not act in this manner, for Māyā is subject to transformation;
indeed, no distinction between agents is established by means of either mental modifications (vṛtti) or transformations (pariṇāma).
Even while constructing a hut, the intellect is indeed seen to be conceptual;
the reality of sound is speech without sound, the eternal Brahman, Kuṇḍalinī.
The teachers have declared that the supreme power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) is *nāda*, also called *mahāmāyā*;
likewise, *bindu* is described as *vyoman* and *anāhata*.
It has four modes of operation by which the three kinds of atoms are pervaded:
Vaikharī, that known as Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and that designated as Sūkṣmā.
Among these, that *vaikharī* speech which expresses meaning is apprehended by the ear;
it assumes the form of articulated phonemes when the vital air is directed toward the points of articulation.
This [speech] of speakers is generally bound to the activity of the vital breath;
it is based solely upon the intellect and follows the sequence of phonemes.
But that which consists of internal discursive thought does not reach the ear;
having transcended the activity of the vital breath, it exists as that called "intermediate" (madhyamā).
Through the process of total withdrawal of all phonemes without differentiation,
Paśyantī is self-luminous, resembling the fluid within a peacock's egg.
Within [the self], there is the light of one's own essential nature, the subtle and inseparable speech;
when that [nature] is perceived, all [worldly] authority ceases.
[AGH: Furthermore, precisely because of the absence of discriminative knowledge regarding that object, the proponents of Śabdabrahman consider it to be inherent in the Person (puruṣa). Thus he says:
They call that which is named "Immortal" to be in the Person consisting of sixteen parts;
it is absolute bliss, terrible, eternally risen, and the Lord. (SRtp 78)
Neither setting nor rising, neither weary nor subject to transformation,
the sun whose essence is the Word-Brahman moves within all living beings.
Having pierced through that with the sword of awakening, those who know the Self emerge without hesitation;
the people who know the Self call that very speech "the subtle" (sūkṣmā). [Here, he states the established conclusion: SRtp_80 //
These modes of activity, which are binding by nature, are each restricted to the individual;
for persons do not perceive the self as distinct from these.

According to the scripture, "The Supreme Self alone is the essence of speech" and "Speech itself is the Self," Vaikharī exists in the cognition produced by the ear, while Madhyamā exists in conceptual cognition.
The visionary [speech] (paśyantī) is perceived during the efforts toward the arising of the intermediate [speech] (madhyamā),
when the recurrence residing in the mind has completely dissolved.
Then, due to non-discrimination, consciousness appears as if subtle and pure;
there is no cognition of atoms that is not accompanied by words.
In this world, all cognition arises as permeated by sound.
(Cf. *Vākyapadīya* I.131:
"There is no cognition in the world that occurs without the accompaniment of sound.")
All knowledge appears as if permeated by sound;
this is the fourfold function based on the kalās such as Nivṛtti and the rest.
Furthermore, it is divided fivefold; those digits (kalās) function as points (bindus):
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and the fifth is Śāntyatītā.
These are the kalās that transcend peace (śāntyatītā), by which the fivefold path is pervaded:
the path of principles (tattvādhvan), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), and that consisting of words (padātmaka).
The path of mantra is pervasive among them, while the path of kalā is supported by the bindu;
having abandoned one by one [the lower levels], one attains the state of being ageless and immortal within the kalās and so forth.
The goal is attained by men; therefore, the paths beginning with *kalā* are [discussed].
The path of *kalā* has been previously described according to its divisions, such as *nivṛtti* and the rest.
I shall explain its pervasion (vyāpti), together with its support, its signs, and its presiding deities,
which has forms and causes, and rests upon the Self, the Bindu, Śakti, and Śiva.
The Nivṛtti-kalā:
In the Nivṛtti [kalā], there is the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) and one hundred and eight cities.
Among them, six—beginning with Kālānala—are outside the infinite cosmic egg (anantāṇḍa).
In each of the ten directions, beginning with the east, there are ten Rudras numbering one hundred, as well as Vīrabhadra above them.
And among the phonemes, the letter *kṣa* is proclaimed to be in the world (*bhuvana*) of Bhadrakālī.
(In this context, the names of the worlds are indeed the same as the names of the Rudras;
and the worlds and so forth have been clearly demonstrated by us in the *Paddhati*).

"The Goddess consists of eighty-one words, according to the sequence of the words of the Pratisarga. [This cross-reference to his *Paddhati* suggests that his commentary on this work may have been composed after 1157 AD. *Śrīkaṇṭhīya-Ṛjuvirmāśinī-tantravyākhyā*, 93.
Established here by means of twenty-eight syllables, she is the mantra-born Heart; therein lies that supreme power (kalā).
Pervading the worlds and so forth, it exists as five within the five;
it is yellow, square, solid, and marked with a thunderbolt.
When that dense mass of many rising rays is meditated upon within the lotus of the heart,
the conceptual construction of the collection of atoms dissolved therein ceases.
Because the fruit has not been attained by that [means], cessation is what is here designated;
Brahman is the cause, and Sadyojāta is the presiding deity.
The *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*:

Within the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], however, there are four; in the *kalā* [of that name], there are the five elements excluding earth (*avanī*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the five organs of action (*karmendriya*).
The five sense organs of cognition, mind, ego, intellect, the unmanifest, and the letters from *ha* to *ṭa* [in reverse order] were present. (SRtp 99)
Twenty-three [evolutes] are enumerated, along with fifty-six cities, [located] within water,
fire, air, ether, intellect, the unmanifest, and the ego-principle.
There are eight [syllables] each, making twenty-one in number;
the two mantras are Śiras and Vāma, and Viṣṇu is said to be the cause.
She, possessing the luster of a white half-moon and marked by blue lotus petals,
should be meditated upon as shining with intense light from within the lotus of her throat.
Because the volition of that [agent], for whom the collection of atoms has dissolved, is established for the sake of accomplishing an object,
that stage is called *Pratiṣṭhā*.
Vāmadeva is indeed considered the presiding deity, consisting of the mantra to be recited.
Regarding the *vidyā-kalās*:
within *vidyā* there are seven—Puruṣa, Rāga, and [the principle] conjoined with Niyati. (SRtp 104)
In that [system], however, the principles of Māyā consist of Vidyā, Kalā, and Kāla;
furthermore, twenty-seven worlds beginning with Māyā are to be known. (SRtp 105)
In this context, the seven phonemes beginning with *ña* and ending with *gha* are listed in reverse order:
*gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*.
And the syllables ÑA [in the Vidyā-kalā]; there are twenty words, and the two mantras Śikha and Ghora are established [therein].
Rudra is the cause here; the mantra is Bahurūpa, the presiding deity. She indeed has many flickering rays, is triangular, and is marked with a svastika.
One should meditate on [the deity] within the lotus of the palate, possessing a luster like that of blue collyrium;
for one whose mass of atoms has dissolved therein, conceptual thought has its range in the entirety of objects.
That by which one's own purpose is illuminated is proclaimed as "knowledge" (vidyā).
Regarding the Śāntikalā:
in the Śānti [kalā], there are three principles (tattvas) and eighteen worlds (bhuvanas).
In this context, the three phonemes beginning with *ga* and ending with *na* (i.e., *ka*, *kha*, and *ga*) are considered to be taught [in the *śāntikalā*].
Here there were eleven steps; the two mantras were the face and the armor.
Pervading the worlds and other realms, marked by five [triangles] and six bindus,
it arises from the hexagon with the splendor of a thousand rays ending in a small point.
That supreme Śakti should be meditated upon within the lotus at the center of the eyebrows;
for one whose collection of atoms has dissolved into her, there is an absence of hatred, passion, and the like.
Because of the complete stilling of volitional thought, this is called peace;
in that state, the Lord is the cause, and the mantra is named Tatpuruṣa.
The person who presides over that is to be known as the presiding deity (adhidevatā);
and here there are three principles (tattvas), while the fifth is the supreme aspect (kalā).
The Śāntyatīta-kalā consists of the Śiva-tattva; therein are fifteen cities,
and the sixteen phonemes known as vowels, preceded by the Visarga.
The first word is *oṃ*, and the mantras are designated as Śiva, Astra, and Īśāna;
and the supreme *kalā* is Śāntyatītā, which contains within it the five paths (*pañcādhvan*). (SRtp 116)
The one to be contemplated has the nature of the great space within the lotus of the crown;
Īśāna, the king of mantras, presides over her as the cause.
There, the Lord Sadāśiva is proclaimed as the Path of Kalās;
he is all-pervasive with respect to the worlds and other categories, being fully permeated by the Bindu.
This Bindu is pervaded by Śakti and Śiva, and not by anything else;
for that Lord, having encompassed [all] with his own Śakti who is non-different from him, [pervades it].
Having pervaded everything, she knows and acts;
the existence of one thing in another is always non-deviating.
Pervasion (vyāpti) is the basis for the attainment and maintenance of the nature of the objects of authoritative testimony;
it is twofold: one [is based] on proximity, and the other from the injunction of the Supreme Self.
In that regard, consciousness brings about everything through its mere presence,
just as the sun is beneficial to all daily activities by virtue of its proximity.
Impelled by Śiva, the Bindu brings about all six paths, beginning with Nāda, within the Self through those various transformations in due order.
Just as clay jars and other such objects, when presided over by a potter, themselves transform so as to pervade whatever object is [intended] by that [potter]; SRtp 124.
That is said to be its transformation, just as a crown is a transformation of gold;
it is that which is pervaded by the *bindu*, the sixfold path beginning with *kalā*.
That manifestation [of Śiva] is not distinct from Him because it is pervaded by Him, like a sound or a drop;
some declare that the *bindu* is inherent within Śiva.
This supreme Kuṇḍalinī is the power of action, just like the power of vision;
these two powers, consisting of knowledge and action, are inherent in Śiva.
But primordial consciousness is cognition, action, and the supreme Kuṇḍalinī;
through the power of knowledge she cognizes, and through action she creates the universe.
For action alone bestows fruit upon men; knowledge does not grant fruit.
He is never separated from those two, and they do not exist without Śiva.
When those two expand in equilibrium, he becomes Sadāśiva, whose essence is reality;
[this occurs] when the powers of action (kriyā-śakti) and knowledge (jñāna-śakti) exceed [the power of will], with Īśvara being predominant.
Within those principles (tattvas), there are diverse worlds belonging to the great-souled ones who are liberated through pure consciousness; their beloveds delight in their innate natures.
Śiva bestows upon his non-differentiated power, whose nature is action, both enjoyments that never fade and the limbs and organs [of the body].
Because he is the agent even of [the principles] beginning with Nāda, he is considered the creator of the pure path (śuddhādhvan).
Therefore, he is not separate from Śakti; rather, Śakti itself is of the nature of action (kriyātmikā).
In that state, O Śivā, it is designated as the *bindu* when it is fully integrated;
this very [bindu], within the Self, [perceives] the multitude of principles and the series of many worlds.
Producing various and manifold things such as bodies, enjoyments, and sense organs,
that which is called the *bindu* is logically described as undergoing transformation, just like the *pradhāna*.
Whatever entity is subject to transformation is necessarily insentient by nature;
just as milk [is insentient], how could there be an inherence of such insentience in Śiva?
For that relation of identity, if it were with something insentient,
would bring about insentience in Śiva, whose singular nature is an incomparable, indivisible mass of consciousness.
But for that dull-witted person who, out of delusion, considers the insentient world to be the Lord—for him there is neither logic nor scripture, neither a self nor a deity. (SRtp 138)
This [view] must be avoided by the wise, as it is excluded from all affirmative systems (sarvāstika),
because action is the cause [of bondage], and since the power of action is consciousness itself.
If it is argued that there is no other Bindu above Māyā because it is insentient,
then from where would the pure path arise, where would it dissolve, or by what means?
This [reality] is sixfold through the divisions of the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), and so forth.
How and why, moreover, are the Vijñānakevalas threefold? 141.
They could not be liberated without the *bindu*, which brings about that diversity;
for consciousness does not effect that [liberation] entirely through transformation.
That it exists because of the nature of consciousness will be stated later in the *Śaktinirṇaya*;
furthermore, we have established this at length in the *Tattvaprakāśavṛtti*.
(The commentary on this work is posterior to the *Tattvaprakāśavṛtti*.)
The objection of another: "This [Self] may possess many imagined distinctions due to its various effects. (SRtp 143)
If it is thought that Śiva is indeed one and possesses manifold powers, then the path belonging to Māyā would likewise be so, since there is no difference in the underlying logic.
How could a wise person reject the pure paths established by their respective causes, scriptures, and even the direct perceptions of yogins?
In the case of a distinguished lord who is a most noble donor,
activity according to the scriptures is said to lead both to enjoyment and to liberation.
The state of Sadāśiva is attained through yoga, or through conduct, or through initiation;
liberation is attained through the differentiation of the mind, or else through all four.
[Note: This is a quotation from Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 26:63.
Thus, experience is fully described as the great state of Sadāśiva;
there, no further substrate of illusion arises, such as the body, objects of experience, and so forth. (SRtp_148)
Therefore, because of its purity, the pure path (śuddhādhvan) is established for the purpose of enjoyment;
furthermore, Māyā is presided over by some agent who is the one to be employed.
She is the material cause of the *kalās* and so forth, her very nature being pervaded by the *kalās*,
just as clay is for pots and other vessels by the potter.
The individual soul is to be employed by means of its state as a sacrificial animal; Maheśvara is the agent and the cause.
This living being is proclaimed to be ignorant and lacking self-mastery even with respect to its own actions.
Cf. Vāyavīya Purāṇa 5.63:
This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed into a pit.
This is quoted in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* under the section on the Śaiva Darśana on page 176 of the third edition of Abhyankar’s text (BORI, 1978);
it also occurs in the *Mahābhārata* 3.31.
And it is cited as *Āgamaḍambara* 3:30 and in *Nyāyamañjarī* I, p. 511.
Also cf. Pauṣkara 1:86:

"O best of the twice-born, since this living being is ignorant and lacks independent mastery over itself, it too must be dependent [on another] for its own activity, just like a jar or similar objects. (86)
Whether one performs a good or an evil deed, it is impelled by the Lord;
being subject to His direction, the infinite soul is joined with a body and so forth, just like a potter [with his wheel and tools].
That path by which Māyā is agitated— through the body, the senses,
and the location and so forth— is purified in the teaching of Śiva.
Other wise scholars call this state of the *bindu* "māyā," because its essential nature is pervaded by *kalās* and it is presided over by the *pudgala*.
In the same way, their primordial nature (prakṛti) is threefold—gross, subtle, and supreme; therein, the gross form is Mahāmāyā, consisting of the [three] guṇas.
That Prakṛti is the producer of the objects of enjoyment, such as the intellect and so forth, for the Puruṣa;
she is subtle, consisting of the undifferentiated nature of the principles beginning with Kalā.
The deluding Māyā is the mother, the cause of the entire impure path;
she is the supreme source of mantras, the eternal Kuṇḍalinī.

This Māyā, which consists of effects and is subject to transformation, is the material cause (*upādāna*) of bodies whose selves are the lords of knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and ignorance (*avidya*). SRtp_158 //
Then one should establish the agent as being conjoined with the body and the senses;
thereafter, the accomplishment of the pure path stands as inevitable.
For those who hold that Māyā is impermanent and is the cause of the *kalās*, *avidyā*, and so forth,
the path of Asita is not purified by the purification of the *kalās*.

For the five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, when purified, lead to the purification of the principles (tattvas) and so forth; therefore, the path (adhvan), specifically that which pertains to the Bindu, is the effect [of this purification].
However, purity in the paths is not considered to arise from the purity of the mere pervaders;
for the *kalās* are of a non-appropriating nature, while the two [principles] are eternally pure.
Because the constant state of purity follows from the very purification of Śiva and Śakti,
this supreme Mahāmāyā is declared to be the primordial nature of all the paths.
By those teachers who are experts in the doctrine of the activity of all paths,
others, however, declare here that Māyā is the sound of the path that is imperishable.
Those who know the scriptures should understand that the purification of the *kalās* and other elements, which are pervaded by the *bindu*, is likewise [to be understood] as such.
Through that very purity which is all-pervasive, there is purification based on the other;
she is Mahāmāyā, the source of mantra, who abides in the state of universal embrace.
This power of Śiva, by which all individuals are pervaded, is this very power whose nature is action; she is the Sovereign Goddess, eternally manifest.
Existing among the bound souls (paśus) itself, established as their fetter (pāśa),
it constantly causes the bound souls to revolve, unsettled within various wombs.
Through the power of self-reflection, she bestows both enjoyment and liberation;
she is the cause for the arising of the conditions that serve as the means for achieving enjoyment.
Interwoven with words, it always deludes the undiscriminating,
perpetually creating a sense of separation from the attainment of the immortal.
Then, for the bound soul whose mind was longing for the pleasure of enjoying sense objects,
knowledge became the preparatory means for the cause of the supreme nectar.
And that [universe] arose from the mass of sound through the interpenetration of speech;
the mass of sound arose from the point (*bindu*), and that point arose from the resonance (*nāda*).
This [unstruck sound] at the Bindu is the cause of the pure path;
therein, by way of being the enjoyer, one experiences through the enjoyments that are the objects of the body and the senses.
Impurity, action, and māyā are inferred to be pure;
indeed, pure māyā alone is the cause of both impurity and action.
When both are impure, impurity itself is considered to be twofold due to *māyā*;
through the discernment of the *bindu*, the shell of impurity is suddenly shattered.
But through the discernment of the illusory person, there occurs the destruction of the husks of merit and demerit;
one perceives oneself as having transcended illusion, yet still connected to the Great Illusion.
The power of the Lord exists for the sake of agitating the Bindu,
just as the ocean is stirred only on its surface by the friction of the wind.
In this way, from a single part, a drop of power pervades the whole;
likewise, by means of a single portion of Māyā, it transforms the entire universe.
In the same way, the unmanifest (avyakta) is held to pervade its own effect;
therein, when it is undisturbed, there occurs experience within the drop (bindu), which is of the nature of bliss.
When [the bindu] is agitated, the Lord has authority; dissolution occurs when it has transcended the bindu. Indeed, there is only one power of consciousness (cicchakti) inherent in Śiva.
Due to the differentiation of the three kinds of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), [the Goddess] is the one who presides over dissolution, enjoyment, and authority;
through connection with these three, the single God becomes threefold.
Śiva is Sadāśiva, the Supreme Lord who possesses the powers of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority;
his Śakti consists of a vast and unimpeded mass of rays.
Ever-risen and uninterrupted, her nature is free from conceptual construction;
she possesses a majesty that is unconditioned, beyond dualities, and requires no material cause.
Arising as a transformation through connection with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
it is most capable of pervading the *bindu*— the manifold of phenomena (*prapañca*) that is both quiescent and emergent.
Independent of others, not to be manifested by another self, facing in all directions,
devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and free from all bonds.
The ultimate limit, the supreme, the subtle, and that which intensely delights in the mere reality—
consciousness alone is considered the undecaying majesty of the Supreme Lord.
In the very presence of Śiva, who possesses no previously acquired specific qualities,
there occurs through this [power] a specific connection characterized by its eternal nature.

The *bindu*, repeatedly filling the individual space of consciousness (*āṇava-cin-nabhaḥ*) with the sounds of resonance (*nāda*), transforms it as if concealing it with its various modes of activity (*vṛtti*).
Just as the ocean, through its connection with the moon in the presence of the sun, transforms by means of its surging waves while filling the sky with sound; so too does the mind.
This very power, which has Śiva as its locus, is unfailing and full of strength;
though it is one, it is perceived as if divided into many according to the diversity of its effects.
Just as the single power of the Sun, through its acts of giving and taking,
performs both what is desired and what is undesired, so too is the imperishable Consciousness (cit) the Will (icchā).
Thus, even ignorance takes the form of knowledge, and likewise, even non-action becomes action;
for whatever is its effect is determined by both tradition and the world.
Thus, this embodied Power, possessing inconceivable majesty, accomplishes [all things];
even a single wish-fulfilling tree bestows many desires.
And just as the wish-fulfilling gem possesses various and inconceivable powers of greatness,
so too does [the intellect], whose singular nature is not endowed with any specific mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
The inconceivable power of the All-pervading Lord, which effects all purposes without exception, is neither born nor does it die; it neither wanes nor does it wax.
Consciousness is power because it is luminous and non-inert; furthermore, that which arises or perishes, and which accumulates or diminishes, [is not consciousness].
Just as the body and so forth are seen to be either non-luminous in nature or insentient, so too is this [Self] not like them; therefore, it is not subject to modification.
By those very two arguments, transformation is refuted;
for it is observed that there is a transformation of the power of consciousness into non-consciousness.
Resorting to that which is unchanging, unfading, eternal,
and auspicious through the relation of identity (tādātmya) by means of inherence (samavāya), consciousness is indeed not subject to transformation.
This [Sattva] is eternal because it is the cause of all effects, just like Īśvara;
furthermore, it is said to be like the *bindu* because it is devoid of a cause for its own existence.
For it is by depending upon her that other virtuous beings are established as eternal;
for when she is established, the world is established, and when she is not established, nothing at all exists.
Of what is its existence established, or by whom is it made known?
Some wise ones proclaim this very [reality] to be non-dual.
Consciousness, which possesses the radiant manifestation of the transformations of both the existent and the non-existent,
is like a rope that causes the illusion of a series of holes where none exist.
It does not produce those objects that are non-existent; rather, it manifests them.
In this same way, this [consciousness], which is mere cognition, appears as one or many due to delusion.
This delusion is without objective basis and contradicts all principles of logic;
because its root has been severed through investigation, it is not the cause of either bondage or liberation.
Therefore, upon investigation, there is neither the bound, nor the bond, nor another who binds;
there exists only the eternally liberated, non-dual, infinite consciousness alone.
But how, then, is this appearance of differentiation perceived?
Conventional practice, however, should be understood as having the nature of differentiation, like a yakṣa in a banyan tree.
For indeed, the differentiation of entities is not perceived by sensory cognition,
since it arises from objects without conceptual construction, just like the consciousness of infants, the mute, and others.
She is the ordainer of all things and does not negate anything whatsoever.
The wise say that perception is an affirmer, not a negator;
for that cognition which possesses qualifiers is preceded by the mental processing of words.
That cognition arising from the capacity of the object itself was not produced again by the senses depending on place, time, and so forth; it is considered to be like memory or conceptualization.
In that case, inference and scripture are not valid means of cognition because they are absent;
for even when the object is conceptualized, it is perception alone that [cognizes] that very object.

Therefore, the one of deluded intellect is bound by the nooses of doubt arising from himself; yet he is liberated from those very same nooses. In reality, however, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Thus, those possessed by the grasping at non-duality, while prattling on, are enlightened by compassionate gurus who bestow the established tenets and the scriptures.
If this non-dual consciousness were established by means of conventional instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
it would certainly become dualistic by virtue of those very same instruments.
The subject, the example, and the reason are each well-established in themselves;
yet, when augmented by pervasion (vyāpti), they serve to establish a property that is not yet established.
A property that is already established is not being proven, nor is it so by those [reasons] that are unestablished;
furthermore, establishment and non-establishment cannot coexist in a single locus.
If there were a difference between the similar class (sapakṣa) and the subject (pakṣa), inference would be the means of valid cognition;
for if they were identical, there could be no similarity of the reason (hetu-sādharmya) due to the absence of that [difference].
"To establish non-duality [the opponent asks], 'Whose pervasion is it, by what, and how? Yet the formal argument (prayoga) employed to achieve its own purpose reveals duality."
In that view, even the negation "non-dual" would be applicable to consciousness;
therefore, duality would necessarily be established elsewhere, even if [consciousness] were established.
Their thesis is undermined, being manifested as a mere wishful thought; even scripture is [invalidated] because those various words merely recall specific meanings already known.
How could it express the collection of objects as qualified by their mutual relations, if this non-dual consciousness were intended to be expressed by itself? (SRtp 221)
How can scripture establish non-duality, or even inference,
when it is being obstructed by its own constituent parts, which are capable of destroying that very non-duality?
Furthermore, words are observed in both worldly and Vedic usage to abandon their primary meaning due to contradiction and to function instead in a secondary sense.

Statements such as "this Brāhmaṇa is a cow" or "the sacrificial post is the sun" do not function as valid reasons; for if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not perceived, they cannot establish the probandum (*sādhya*). (SRtp 224)
Therefore, scriptural passages overcome by the force of reasoning abandon even their primary meaning and offer praise for the unity of selves.
Even non-conceptual perception grasps the particularity of an object,
by virtue of which it arises in the form of a distinction from other things.
Arising preceded by the recollection of specific names and so forth, it is conceptual, free from doubt, and devoid of error. (SRtp 227)

Cognition designated as "direct perception" would otherwise be untenable for one who has not grasped the distinction between objects, just like that [cognition] which possesses specific names and so forth.
The efficacy of inference also depends upon the apprehension of difference;
for if there were a connection through the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding the universal (*sāmānya*).
Moreover, if one accepts the otherness of non-duality and difference, then difference would be established; yet, in this way, it is precisely the state of non-otherness that is proven.
For the probandum cannot be established by a mere example;
therefore, the illustration of the rope serves only to confuse the disciple.
Nor is consciousness equal to the rope, because its specific distinctions are not perceived;
it is that which undergoes transformation through those entities which bring about the cessation of mere cognition.
But she, though known through direct experience, manifests herself as various entities for the bound soul whose power of vision is obstructed by impurity, just as the moon appears so to a man.
[Note: The example of the moon in water, again for the sake of *vivarta*:
Just as one afflicted by cataracts, even while reasoning by means of a thousand arguments, [does not perceive the true nature of the moon].
One repeatedly beholds that single moon as many moons again and again.
Or, just as one whose sense of taste is corrupted by bile perceives even bitter milk as sweet when imagining it to be sweet,
due to a defect in the sensory faculty.
Or just as when water mixed with collyrium is being boiled,
even for the wise, there arises the non-discriminative cognition of it as both blue and hot.
Thus, having been correctly examined through scriptures accompanied by logical reasoning,
it is seen to arise, to perish, and to manifest in various ways.
One should bring about the removal of the obscuration of knowledge through the cause [of devotion], just as one removes cataracts and the like;
and that [removal] occurs by means of devotion to Śiva as proclaimed in the Śiva scriptures.
It can be turned back by action alone and not otherwise, even by millions of pieces of knowledge,
just as cataracts and the like are cured only by the medical treatment prescribed in the treatises on health.
Even when there is a difference in place, time, and person,
how could a manifestation (vivarta) of consciousness be something that does not appear otherwise [than as consciousness] and is uncontradicted by the means of valid cognition?
Furthermore, the manifold world (prapañca) is established as being illusory (māyeya) by means of the very instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Therefore, consciousness (saṃvit) evolves [into this world] solely due to the bondage of the atoms (aṇu).
Indeed, *vivarta* is the false transformation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*),
by which that [power], though not possessing that form, is experienced as if it were endowed with that form.
This [world], which consists of the realms of consciousness and unconsciousness and is mutually connected,
arises through non-discrimination because it is established by the mutual superimposition of those two.

In that regard, consciousness— remaining itself unchanging— superimposes upon its own nature the fluctuations and modifications belonging to the intellect (buddhi), due to the non-discrimination between the intellect and the reality of consciousness.
Following birth and so forth, [the intellect] shows the individual soul its own self as "born," "perished," "various," "possessing happiness," and "possessing suffering."

In the same way, by superimposing insentience upon the Self and attributing the quality of consciousness to it through non-discrimination, one thinks, "I am the knower," and "I am thin. Thus, [the fool acts]. (SRtp 246)
This non-discrimination of all atoms is caused by impurity.
The root of the continuum dominated by delusion is the [apprehension] of the conscious and the insentient as distinct entities.

For it is not logical that there should be a distinction of illusory transformations (*vivarta*) between specific cognitions and distinct insentient objects, in the absence of a firm connection between them.

For instance, the notion of "I" occurs with respect to the body and not with respect to a clod of earth; moreover, that notion belongs to someone [specific] and not to everyone, as it arises only for the individual soul (aṇu). Therefore, bondage is held to belong to those two [the soul and the mind].
Whatever sense organs belong to a person for the sake of knowledge and action,
those same organs do not function as instruments for those two activities for anyone else.
Only a specific cognition is prevented from undergoing transformation for a particular conscious being;
not every cognition of everyone. Therefore, bondage is held to belong to those two [the specific cognition and its substrate].
Whatever pleasure or pain, however slight, is mounted upon the intellect and experienced by a person through some means or other, by that [experience] their bondage is determined.
If non-discrimination is the controller, then by what is it produced in those two [the soul and the intellect] alone?
By that [non-discrimination], bondage exists; and bondage is considered to be entirely distinct from the Lord.
The bound soul is deluded in nature; liberation is the release from that bondage.
When bondage has dissolved in every respect and the *āṇava* impurity has been cast off, [one is liberated].
The power that illuminates all objects is the very unfolding of Śiva;
this most exalted power is entirely free from all obscurations.
Enveloping a very small portion of the objective field, that [power] manifests it;
for there is no bondage for the power whose nature is supreme consciousness.
Only the Supreme (paramātra) would shine incessantly for liberated souls;

that is to say, because they are free from impurity (mala), the consciousness of the liberated self—which illuminates both itself and others—would manifest only the Supreme as the mere existence (sattāmātra) of the ultimate reality.
However, unlike bound souls, it does not manifest through specific objects of enjoyment. This is the meaning.
If that were the case, it would follow that even the liberated would be enjoyers due to their experiencing pleasure, pain, and so forth;
therefore, the liberated are omniscient, but not perceivers of mere consciousness alone.
If an external object exists, that ignorance regarding the reality would be caused by darkness;
for those who are veiled by darkness do not become liberated.
Conceptual construction arises for individual souls obstructed by impurity during the perception of objects through the piercing of sound, due to the agitation of the *bindu*. (SRtp 259)

From the non-disturbance of the stainless *bindu*, there arises the realization of the object free from conceptual construction, born from the bondage and liberation of that [bindu], like a child born on that very day.
Whatever entity exists at any time— whether past or future— it exists as such at that very moment.
The imperishable consciousness, self-cognizable, perceives the state of things as they truly are.
They are not the creators of the universe, for Śiva alone is its creator;
indeed, no evidence whatsoever exists anywhere for a plurality of creators.
Perpetually liberated, eternally manifest, and possessing inconceivable power, that which is designated as Śakti constantly rests upon Śiva, the supreme cause.
Having pervaded that [Māyā], the Lord creates, sustains, and destroys;
He conceals Himself and bestows grace upon His own [souls].
Regarding those tasks to be performed, the agent is said by the teachers to be of three kinds in five ways:
the capable, the one who has undertaken effort, and the one who has set forth.
[An allusion to the statement: "The agent is held to be threefold: capable, prepared, and engaged," as quoted in the *Kiraṇāvalī* (ad *Māṭhara-vṛtti* on *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* 3.2.0).]
And as stated in the *Śataratnasaṅgraha* 14: "And note that here too it is attributed to humans by the teachers (*deśikaiḥ*).
"In that regard, the first [power] is capable and designated as the partless Śiva (*niṣkala-śiva*). Within Him, the sovereign power known as Action (*kriyā*) remains as if in a bud. (SRtp 266)
That very [power], awakening and languid with the weight of the attained essence within the *bindu*,
loudly manifests for her husband a continuous flow of supreme bliss.
That glorious Lord, who is both with parts and without parts, whose body consists of the five mantras, and who is ever auspicious, constantly delights in her, being perpetually engaged in union.
Because it involves the contemplation of all phenomena and provides protection from the ocean of saṃsāra,
the power of that [mantra] is indeed of the nature of mantra, characterized by the qualities of contemplation and protection.

As it has been said: "Thinking (manana) is omniscience, and protection (trāṇa) is the favoring of transmigrating beings; because they possess the qualities of thinking and protecting, they are designated as *mantra*. And this etymological derivation applies equally to Śiva, to His Power (Śakti), and to the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) and others.
And for this reason, the term "mantra" is applied metaphorically to expressive words:
due to the difference in function and by virtue of its substrata, that single [Reality] appears in five ways,
having as its sphere the five substrata to be presided over, beginning with Bindu and Śānti.
Bindu, Śānti, Kalā, Vidyā, and Nivṛtti along with Pratiṣṭhā—these five are the stations of experience for them; the designation "Bindu" is proclaimed by Śiva.
This undivided state of the five kalās is designated as the Bindu;
its sphere is the supreme form (parā mūrti), while the non-supreme (aparā) has the realm of effects as its sphere.
That stainless power which is inherent in Śiva is itself his form; due to the differentiation of its functions, it is called the body known as Sādākhya.
Mahāmāyā was fully pervaded by the powerful Śiva,
[the state] of those stainless ones whose nature is Śiva and who are established in the abode of enjoyment.
That which produces the body, objects of enjoyment, the sense organs, the locus, consciousness, and so forth, is the effect; that power of action is also described in the same way.
Indeed, the power of the Wielder of the Trident is one, consisting of all knowledge and action;
for from it arise will, knowledge, action, and the rest, which are the sources of all effects.
Likewise, for the Īśvaras and Śivas, their bodies, senses, and so forth, consist of Mahāmāyā; they are pure, auspicious, and possessors of their own specific offices.
This power, consisting of action, is inseparable from Śiva;
through connection with it, Śiva is said to be the cause of all effects without exception.
Descending from the Bindu and surrounded by Aṇu and Sadāśiva,
he [establishes] Sadāśiva and Maheśvara in the offices of the duties of the Lord.
Sending forth [his power] along the entire path, the Lord shines at its summit;
Śiva is the tranquil Lord whose face is the five streams and whose head is Śakti.
His large eyes are vision, action, and will; he is endowed with the digit of the moon of consciousness;
his head is Īśāna, his face is the Puruṣa, and his circle of arms extends through the ten directions.
With the Aghora heart-mantra, the Vāma secret-mantra, and the Jāta body-mantra blazing forth,
this God is active, possessed of all parts, and the purifier of all.
NOTE that this marks the conclusion of the commentary on the half-verse cited in 265: *śaktodyuktaḥ prav�ttas ca kartā trividha iṣyate*.
Note also that these last two verses may be considered a paraphrase of *Parākhyatantra* 2:84–85b or of *Mataṅgavṛttipaddhati* (MatVP) 4:14c–15b:
"Śiva alone is thus [the cause], and his Śakti is likewise immutable."
For those two, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, [are present] within the domains of dissolution and enjoyment.
For thus, within the stainless, noble, and profound great ocean of consciousness, they dissolve into their own self; therefore, some are established in meditative absorption (samādhi).
Others, their own powers restrained by Śiva, lie down;
others, embracing Mahāmāyā, remain active.
Those who are greedy for enjoyments, whose intellects are one-pointedly focused on the pleasure arising from contact with that [object],
likewise resort to the supreme ether at the summit of the path.
Following the command of their Lord, they perform the fivefold functions;
therefore, even one among them who possesses the authority for both dissolution and enjoyment [is so].
Through its status as the presiding subject, power attains a figurative distinction; it is considered to be exactly like that [the Self]. Now, the distinction between these two is being stated.
In the pure path, Śiva is the agent; Śakti is the dependent cause.
He should be known as the common substratum, consisting of his own dense, self-abiding consciousness.
That consciousness, however, arises as a craving to grasp all objects;
it is the nature of supreme sovereignty, and its majesty consists in the form of pervasion.
This Great Lord is the great pervader of all objects for those two;
it is that consciousness, known as Śiva, whose nature is independent of anything else.
The wise say that its power is a form dependent on something else:
the perception of two aspects of every single object.
Power residing in Śiva exists both dependent and independent [of other causes],
because it belongs to the Lord whose manifestation is eternally arisen and uninterrupted.
In the case of the object of knowledge, that which is to be governed, the effect, and so forth, there is no further cause or the like;
therefore, it is logical that the power of the Lord is a nature that depends upon another.
This [nature] would not be a mere form dependent upon another for everything,
because forms such as "son" or "effect" are perceived in quite a different way.
But knowledge is not devoid of an object; that very [knowledge] is the grasping of the object. Nor is it so because of contradiction or synonymy, since even in this case, it is imperishable.
This is the nature of perishable things: that they do not arise otherwise at another time;
whereas that which is indestructible is held to be eternal, and for this reason it is distinct from them.
Śambhu exists as the locus of power (śakti), and he likewise exists within her;
thus, by virtue of the limiting adjuncts of effects (kāryopādhi), the designation "power" may even apply to that which is a mass of consciousness (cidghana).
However, some maintain that in reality there is no power dependent on another;
for if one were to produce an effect without an instrument, one would be a creator [in the absolute sense]. (SRtp 299)
This view is indeed improper, as it is contradicted by both reasoning and perception;
moreover, if an unperceived limiting condition were to govern the effect of the Lord...
How could Śiva be free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi) if he is always possessed of existence? Or how could he be an agent if he is devoid of causal knowledge?
Or how could the person perceive the intellect without that power?
Without the lamp of power in between, all this would be blinding darkness.
If another [power] were to arise, what could the Blessed One do, being powerless?
Furthermore, although it is non-different from Śambhu, power is nevertheless held to be distinct.
Just as a lentil seed is not distinct from the thumb, nor is it non-distinct, according to the reasons already stated.
Aghora’s first sentence:
Just as a particular grain called *masūra*, though belonging to the same genus as that which is called the thumb, is distinguished from it by some form or other,

so too, even though there is no difference in substance between Śiva and Śakti, their distinction is established by way of the relationship between the substratum (*dharmin*) and its attribute (*dharma*).
Though non-different from Śambhu, she is distinct from him as his inherent power (samavāyinī).
And its innate radiance, rooted in that [nature], is stainless like the light of the sun;
for this Blessed One does not [possess] a power that is absolutely distinct from his own self.
Sometimes he performs some action, yet he knows nothing at all;
even though he possesses no specific distinction, the god Maheśvara is the cause.
Even the differentiation of effects arises from specific states of the effect;
this drop (bindu), impelled by the power of Śiva, is that in which the effect has dissolved.
For the sake of creation, maintenance, and the dissolution of the manifold world of the Creator,
it is indeed the Bindu alone, having long established the universe, that proceeds [in these functions].
Just as clay, having reached a different state, begins to form a jar,
so too does this [consciousness] previously, by attaining another state of being.
Overwhelmed by the power of the Lord, [the universe] is capable of producing various effects through its diverse modes of activity, even though the wielder of the trident is changeless.

Even though it has not undergone transformation, [the seed] possesses the distinctions of division, drying, and powdering, which arise from the different stages occurring in the sequence already described.
Just as the lotus has the sun as its creator and Śiva likewise [is the cause],
so too the Creator (Vidhātṛ) is the agent of tasks such as creation, being both changeless and yet possessed of power.
Just as the sun, though itself unchanging, is the cause of the rapid liquefaction and drying of beeswax—which is soft and requires no external effort—in an instant; SRtp_313 //

Likewise, even the non-modification of the atoms known as karma— whether equal or unequal, belonging to oneself, and consisting of merit or demerit— is auspicious, for it brings about both bondage and liberation.
When two karmas, whose ripening has been suspended through mutual contradiction,
meet in conjunction, the power of Śiva descends upon the individual soul.
A straightforward affirmation of the *karmasāmyapakṣa* (the position of the equalization of karma), notwithstanding what Agha’s commentary may state (and not the *malaparipākapakṣa*).
As soon as that [mirror] has fallen away, one perceives oneself with the dense veil shaken off, with the turbidity of stains completely stilled.
For he is liberated at that very moment when he is smelled by the will of Śiva;
thereafter, he engages solely in obligatory and occasional rites.
With this very body, the great-souled and blessed Śiva-yogins attain the supreme, unbroken pervasion. (SRtp 318)
Furthermore, he purifies rivers, provinces, gardens, cities, and so forth by his very glance, speech, conduct, and touch, through his effortless grace.
How much more so this person who has come for refuge, terrified by worldly existence!
Homage to our teacher Śivatejas, who is of such a nature!
To the treasury of the jewels of yoga that bestow infinite fruits,
by one whose mind has been purified by the *Āloka* composed by Rāmakaṇṭha.
This *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā* has been composed by Śrīkaṇṭha Sūri,
who here follows the excellent commentary of Śrī Rāmakaṇṭha;
thus, the meaning of the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā* has been elucidated in brief.
Thus ends the Examination of the Three Jewels.
